Virginia. A state on the Atlantic coast of the eastern United States, historically among America's most influential and consequential regions. Situated on the southeastern coast and bordered by North Carolina, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, Maryland, and the District of Columbia, it has shaped American politics, slavery, and democracy.

Virginia was the site of early English colonization. Jamestown, founded in sixteen oh-seven by English settlers, was the first permanent English settlement in North America. It established the first representative assembly, the House of Burgesses, in sixteen nineteen and pioneered the plantation economy based on African slave labor.

Virginia was one of the thirteen original colonies and a powerhouse in the independence movement. It hosted the Continental Congress, produced revolutionary leaders including George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Patrick Henry, and witnessed the British surrender at Yorktown in seventeen eighty-one. Thomas Jefferson, Virginia-born author of the Declaration of Independence and the third U.S. president, exemplified Virginia's intellectual influence. Other Virginia-born presidents include George Washington and James Madison and James Monroe.

Throughout the antebellum era, Virginia was a slave state. Enslaved Africans made up a large portion of Virginia's population and labor force, producing immense wealth for planter elites while creating the moral contradictions of a slave-owning republic. This contradiction would define much of American history.

Virginia was a primary battleground of the American Civil War from eighteen sixty-one to eighteen sixty-five. Cities including Richmond, the capital of the Confederacy, Petersburg, and the Shenandoah Valley saw repeated, devastating campaigns. Robert E. Lee and the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia fought some of the war's bloodiest battles there. Richmond, sitting on the James River, was burned during Union General William Sherman's campaign and later rebuilt into a modern city.

Modern Virginia remains economically and politically significant. It includes the Washington, D.C. suburbs, a booming region, and hosts major military installations including the Pentagon and naval bases. It is also a key swing state in U.S. presidential elections, meaning its political allegiances shape national politics. The state connects to its founding through the Potomac River, which forms its northern and eastern boundary and flows to Washington, D.C., the nation's capital.
